R07-B-01: Few kinds of article travel as easily as the list of untranslatable words. A language is said to possess a single word for the particular light that falls through leaves, another for the guilty pleasure of buying books one will never read, a third for the melancholy of a Sunday evening, and the reader is invited to marvel that English, or whatever language the list happens to be written in, has nothing to match them. The lists are charming, and most of the words in them are real. What is doubtful is the conclusion they are usually taken to support: that the speakers of a language without such a word cannot quite have the experience it names, or that a vocabulary is a window onto a national soul. Look at what the lists actually demonstrate. Each entry pairs a foreign word with a sentence or two of English explaining it, and the explanation is usually clear enough that the reader recognises the experience at once, often with a small shock of familiarity. The list, in other words, translates every word it calls untranslatable. What it shows is not that a meaning cannot cross from one language to another but that one language packages in a single word what another expresses in a phrase. That is a fact about how vocabularies happen to be divided up, and it tells us very little about what their speakers are able to think or feel. Every language lacks single words for countless things its speakers understand perfectly well. This is not to say that nothing is lost when such a word is carried across. A single word is easy to reach for; a phrase is not. A word that ordinary speakers use daily carries the weight of all those uses, along with a register, a sound and a set of associations that no paraphrase reproduces. The very existence of the word suggests that a community has found the experience worth naming, and that fact is itself a small piece of cultural information. For a translator working on a poem, where sound and compression matter as much as sense, these losses are real and constant, and no amount of explanation in a footnote restores them. But the losses are of degree, not of kind, and they are not peculiar to exotic words. They occur whenever any word is rendered by another, and even within a single language, where no two synonyms carry quite the same associations. Seen this way, the romance of the untranslatable flatters the reader, who feels worldly for knowing the rare word, and it encourages a picture of cultures as sealed rooms whose inhabitants can only be gazed at, never understood. The more modest and more accurate lesson is that translation is always possible and never complete, and that its difficulties lie less in the dictionary than in everything a word drags along with it.
R07-B-02: Whenever a much-loved novel reaches the screen, a familiar verdict follows: the book was better. Behind the verdict there usually lies a checklist. Was the heroine's age changed, a subplot dropped, a minor character merged with another, the ending softened? Each departure is counted as a fault, and the best adaptation, on this view, is simply the one that departs least, as though the novel were a fixed list of facts and the film an attempt, more or less competent, to copy that list onto a different surface. The habit is understandable, since readers who love a book feel protective of it, but as a standard for judging films it rests on a confusion about what an adaptation is. A novel and a film do not tell stories in the same way. A novel can spend twenty pages inside a character's head; a film must find something for the camera to look at. A novel handles time loosely, lingering or summarising as it likes, while a film runs at a pace the viewer cannot slow. To reproduce a book's events faithfully is therefore no guarantee of reproducing what the book does. Imagine a novel narrated by a man whose account of himself the reader slowly learns to distrust. A film that simply stages the events he describes, shot plainly and from the outside, may keep every incident and still lose the book entirely, because the book was never really about the incidents but about the gap between what the narrator says and what the reader comes to see. Conversely, an adaptation that alters a good deal may be truer to its source. A director who invents a visual device to unsettle our trust in what we are shown, framing scenes so that the viewer begins to doubt them, has understood that novel better than one who preserves its plot to the letter. The right question is not how much was kept but whether the film has found its own means of doing what the book did. None of this means that every liberty is defensible. Some adaptations borrow a famous title for its prestige and its ready-made audience while discarding everything that made the book worth adapting, and the complaint against them is fair. But it is fair for a different reason than the checklist suggests. Such films fail not because they changed things but because they changed the wrong things, keeping the label and throwing away the substance. Fidelity, properly understood, is a matter of purpose rather than of inventory, and judging it requires the critic to say what a book was for before complaining about what a film has left out.
R07-B-03: A respectable argument holds that negative criticism of new books is a waste of everyone's time. So many books are published each year that no critic can notice more than a sliver of them; the space a journal devotes to criticism is therefore precious, and to spend it explaining why a book is bad is to deny it to a book that deserves attention. On this view the most damning verdict a critic can deliver is silence. A poor book left unmentioned simply sinks, and nothing is lost except the pleasure that some critics take in wounding. The position has the further appeal of seeming kind, which is no small recommendation in a literary world where writers and critics are often the same people. The argument is tidy, but it quietly assumes that the only job of criticism is to guide readers in choosing what to read. If that were so, the notice of a weak book would indeed be wasted, since a reader who is told merely to skip something has learned nothing that he could use elsewhere. But criticism has always done something besides sorting. A careful account of why a book fails is also an account of what success would have looked like, and in giving it the critic makes public a set of standards that readers can test, dispute and apply for themselves. The reader who follows a well-argued case against a novel he admired may end unconvinced, yet he will read the next novel more alertly. There is a further cost to silence. If critics write only about the books they admire, praise becomes the sole currency of criticism, and like any currency issued without limit it loses its value. A notice that can only ever say yes tells the reader very little, because its enthusiasm is not the outcome of a judgement that could have gone the other way. Readers soon learn to discount it, as they discount the admiring phrases printed on the cover of every new book, and the critic whose praise is sincere is then heard no more clearly than the publicist. The possibility of dispraise is what gives praise its meaning. None of this licenses cruelty, and the case for restraint does have force in one kind of instance. A modest first novel from a small press, which few people will encounter anyway, gains nothing from a public demolition, and neither do its readers. The negative notice earns its space when the book in question is prominent: widely praised, heavily promoted, or likely to shape what others write. There the critic who dissents is not kicking someone who is down but contesting a reputation that is already shaping public taste, and that is among the most useful things criticism can do.
R07-B-04: Arguments about the literary canon are usually conducted as arguments about a list. One side defends a set of books as the best that a tradition has produced; the other replies that the list was drawn up by a narrow group of readers and reflects their tastes and their blind spots. Both sides, for all their hostility, agree on what a canon is: a ranking, a roll of honour, a verdict on quality that can be revised by adding names or striking them out. It is worth asking whether that shared assumption is right. A different account fits the actual history of canons better. On this account a work becomes canonical not because readers judge it excellent but because later writers cannot leave it alone. They answer it, parody it, borrow its situations, quarrel with its conclusions and rewrite it from the point of view of a character it neglected. The canonical work is then the one you must have read in order to understand a great many others; its status is less a medal than a position in a network of replies. This explains something the list model cannot. Canons contain works that almost everyone agrees are clumsy, uneven or dull in long stretches, and they exclude works of great finish that simply provoked no answer. A ranking by quality would not look like that; a record of a conversation would. The account has a consequence for those who wish to change the canon. If canonical status is conferred by later writing rather than by verdict, then a syllabus committee cannot make a book canonical by placing it on a reading list, any more than a critic could remove one by declaring it overrated. What can be done is to put neglected works where future writers will meet them, in print, in translation and in the classroom, and then to wait and see whether they are taken up. Yet the conversational canon is not thereby cleared of the exclusions its critics describe. Who gets to join a conversation depends on who was taught to read, who could find a publisher and whose replies were preserved. A tradition in which most writers came from one class or one sex will have conducted its conversation largely among them, and the canon it produced will reflect that. The conversational account does not answer the critics of the canon; it relocates their complaint, from the judgements of tastemakers to the conditions under which people could write at all, and that is where the remedy, if there is one, must be sought.
R07-B-05: Translators of the great books of the past often remark on a puzzle. The original of an old epic or a classical tragedy does not seem to age; readers return to it century after century and find it as alive as ever. Yet translations of the same work date quickly. A version that seemed fresh to its first readers can sound stiff or quaint within a lifetime, and every generation or two a new one appears, prefaced by the claim that its predecessors have become unreadable. Why should the copy age when the original, which is older and in many ways stranger, does not? The question is worth more attention than it usually receives, because the answer says something about what a translation is. The usual answer is linguistic: a translation is written in the language of its own moment, with that moment's idioms and its notions of what sounds dignified and what sounds plain, and these change. The original, by contrast, has been absorbed into a tradition that reads it as a historical text and forgives its strangeness. There is truth in this, but it cannot be the whole story, since old translations are often perfectly intelligible and still feel inadequate. A deeper reason lies in what translation requires. A great work is full of places where its sense is undecided: a word that could mean anger or grief, a line whose tone could be mocking or tender, a scene whose moral weight is left to the reader. The original can leave such places open, and much of its power to sustain rereading comes from that openness; a translator has no such freedom, because writing in another language forces choices at every point, and each choice settles a question the original left unsettled. The choices are not arbitrary, but they are shaped by what the translator's own age finds plausible or important, and so the translation records one generation's reading of the work. When the concerns of that generation fade, its translation comes to look like what it always was: an interpretation. Seen in this light, retranslation is not a sign that earlier translators failed. It is one of the ways a classic stays alive, each version making a fresh set of decisions and so showing a new reader something the others concealed. There is even an occasional reversal. Some translations become works of literature in their own right, read not as windows onto the original but for their own sake, and these, curiously, stop ageing in the way translations usually do; they come to be read, like originals, as historical texts. Their choices no longer look like a period's reading of another book; they look like the permanent features of a book of their own.
R07-B-06: Few questions in criticism have been argued so long, or with so little sign of settlement, as whether the meaning of a work is what its author intended. The intentionalist says yes: a text is an utterance, utterances are made by someone for a purpose, and to ignore that purpose is to read not the work but a sequence of marks that happens to resemble it. The anti-intentionalist says no: the author's state of mind is usually unavailable, frequently confused and in any case beside the point, since a published work belongs to the public language in which it was written, and its meaning is whatever that language, competently read, makes of it. Each side wins its arguments by making the other's view look absurd, and each is right about what it denies. The intentionalist is right that we cannot read without attributing purposes. To notice that a sentence is ironic, that a repetition is deliberate or that a sudden plainness of style marks a turning point is already to treat the text as the product of choices; strip away every assumption about purpose and the irony vanishes along with the design. The anti-intentionalist is right that a letter to a newspaper or a diary entry in which the author explains what the book means has no special authority over the book. Authors misremember, revise their motives after the fact and sometimes simply misjudge what they have made. The mistake common to both is to picture intention as a private event lying behind the text, which the text either reports faithfully or conceals. Intention in writing is better understood the way we understand it in action. We do not usually discover what someone meant by watching them and then consulting their inner life; we read the purpose in the shape of what they did. In the same way the intentions that matter to criticism are those embodied in a work's choices, its emphases and omissions, the expectations it sets up and then disappoints. They are public because the work is. This view does not make the author irrelevant, nor does it make the author final. A writer's notebooks may help us see a pattern we had missed, as the testimony of a witness may help a court, but the evidence is then the pattern, not the testimony. And a work may carry implications its author never foresaw and would perhaps have disowned: a novel written to celebrate a way of life can, through the very details it lovingly records, reveal the costs that way of life imposed on those at its margins. To point this out is not to defy the author's intention but to take the work's design more seriously than its author's later account of it.
R07-B-07: It is often said that a book can be read for the first time only once, and the remark is usually meant as a lament. On a first reading we do not know what will happen; we are carried by suspense, surprised by turns we did not foresee, and moved in a way that, the argument goes, can never quite be recovered. Rereading, on this view, is a kind of nostalgia: a return to a place whose excitement has been used up, pleasant perhaps, but a lesser thing than the original encounter. Schools encourage the same view without meaning to, since a syllabus moves on once a book has been 'done', as though a single passage through it were the whole of the work. The lament has real feeling behind it, and anyone who remembers staying up late to finish a novel knows what it describes. There is a case for the opposite view, that in an important sense only rereading is reading. A first reading is dominated by one question, what happens next, and that question consumes most of our attention. We skim descriptions to reach events, miss the significance of details whose importance has not yet been revealed and form judgements of characters that the book later overturns. Only when we know the ending can we attend to how the book reaches it: the early scene that quietly prepares a later one, the image that returns with altered meaning, the minor character whose remark, seemingly idle at first, turns out to state the novel's theme. Knowing the outcome does not empty these details; it fills them. Consider a novel built around a concealed secret. Read a second time, its hints, which at first seemed part of the scenery, stand out as hints, and the reader can admire the skill with which they were hidden in plain sight, a pleasure that the first reader, hurrying towards the revelation, could not have had. Rereading also reveals a change in the reader. The novel read at fifteen and again at forty has not altered a word, yet it is a different book, because the person reading it has acquired experiences that let different passages speak. A story of a marriage that seemed, to the young reader, a tale of dull people becomes, to the older one, almost unbearably exact. Nothing on the page has moved; what has moved is the range of experience the reader can bring to it, and with it the passages that seem to matter. In this sense a book reread is a kind of instrument for measuring oneself, and the measurements are often humbling: we discover what we were once unable to see, and sometimes that the passages we admired most were the weakest. None of this means that the first reading is worthless. It has a quality nothing later can supply, an innocence about what is coming that the writer counted on, and some effects are designed for it alone: the twist that recasts everything before it can surprise only once. Moreover, without a first reading there is nothing to reread, and the second encounter depends on the first even when it corrects it. Some books, indeed, are exhausted by one passage through them, and this is perhaps the most useful test of all. A book that offers nothing on a second reading was a mechanism for producing suspense, admirable in its way, while a book that gives more each time was something else. The difference between the two kinds is not visible from inside a first reading, which is one more reason to distrust the verdicts we reach there.
R07-B-08: Literary history has always been written from a remarkably small sample. Of the many thousands of novels published in a given century, a scholar can read a few hundred in a working life, and the histories of the form are built on a smaller set still, the books that later readers chose to keep in print. When such a history says that 'the novel' turned inward at a certain period, or abandoned the omniscient narrator, or grew preoccupied with the city, it is generalising from a selection that was never meant to be representative. Nobody chose the canon as a sample; it was assembled by generations of readers for reasons of taste, teaching and accident, and there is no reason to expect it to resemble the whole from which it was drawn. The advocates of computational or 'distant' reading start from this embarrassment. If machines can process an entire century's output, counting words, tracking the length of sentences or the frequency with which characters are named, then claims about the form as a whole can at last be tested against the whole. The objections are familiar, and some are serious. Counting is not reading. The meaning of a word depends on its context, on irony, on the dramatic situation in which it is spoken, none of which a frequency table records. Critics add that many of the patterns such studies report are either trivial or confirm what attentive readers already knew, so that a great deal of machinery produces a modest result dressed in charts. There is also a subtler worry: the features a computer can count are those that can be defined mechanically, and these are not obviously the features that matter. A discipline that adopts such tools risks drifting towards studying what can be measured simply because it can be measured. Defenders of the method reply that every discipline begins by measuring crude things, but the reply concedes more than it denies. Yet much of this debate rests on a false picture of the choice. Distant reading does not replace close reading so much as change what close reading is asked to do. Its most interesting results are rarely the patterns themselves; they are the anomalies, the decade in which a measure behaves unexpectedly or the obscure novels that cluster with canonical ones on some feature nobody had thought to examine. A measure that shows some habit of style rising steadily for decades and then collapsing within a few years explains nothing by itself, but it tells a scholar exactly where to look. Such a finding means little until someone goes back and reads the books in question, and it is that return which produces understanding. The count poses a question; it does not answer one. Where the method does make an independent contribution is in the matter of the sample. Even if a computer can say little about what any single novel means, it can show that a generalisation drawn from the canon fails to hold for the much larger body of books that the canon left out. That is not a trivial service. A claim about what 'the novel' did, which turns out to describe only the few hundred books that survived into the syllabus, was never a claim about the novel at all, but about the tastes of the readers who did the selecting. The modest promise of distant reading, then, is less to tell us what literature means than to tell us more accurately which literature our claims are about.
